title: Garbage collection concept and memory lifecycle
learningObjectives: Explain garbage collection concept and memory lifecycle and reason about JavaScript execution and function behaviour.

understand.concept: JavaScript engines automatically reclaim memory for objects that are no longer reachable from live references. Garbage collection timing is implementation-dependent. Global references, active closures, event listeners, timers, and caches can keep objects reachable longer than intended.
understand.whyItMatters: Automatic memory management does not prevent leaks. Developers should release resources and references they no longer need, especially in long-running applications.
understand.analogy: Garbage collection is like clearing items that no longer have any path back from the active workspace; a forgotten reference keeps an item in use.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is simplified; JavaScript scope, execution, identity, and scheduling follow language and engine semantics.

explain.narrative: Setting the variable to null removes this reference. The engine decides when to reclaim memory, and any other references keep the object alive.

examples.code: let largeData={items:Array.from({length:1000},(_,i)=>({id:i}))};console.log(largeData.items.length);largeData=null;// The object may become eligible for collection if no other references remain.
examples.explanation: Setting the variable to null removes this reference. The engine decides when to reclaim memory, and any other references keep the object alive.
examples.expectedOutput: Console output demonstrates the language behaviour described.

practise.guidedTask: Find a retained event listener or timer in a sample component and add cleanup. Explain why setting one variable to null may not be enough.
practise.independentTask: Create a small example that demonstrates the concept, test edge cases, and explain the execution or reference behaviour in your own words.
